theory.intro: A **conclusion** is a statement about the world that the data gives you a reason to believe. A conclusion is **supported** when it stays inside what the data actually covers and is backed by evidence you can quote — the statistics themselves. It **overreaches** when it talks about a group that was never surveyed, about something that was never measured, about **why** a change happened, or about what will happen next. Data collected by a **census** covers the whole population, so a conclusion about that population is exact. Data collected by a **sample** describes the part that was surveyed, and only supports a conclusion about the whole population when the sample fairly represents it.
facts: A conclusion is supported only when you can quote evidence for it from the data itself.
Two statistics together give a stronger conclusion than one: a **higher mean and a smaller range** means better on average **and** more consistent.
When the two statistics disagree, say so — one dataset can be higher on average while the other is the more consistent.
A **census** covers every member of the population, so a conclusion about that population is exact.
A **sample** supports a conclusion about the whole population only when it fairly represents that population; a sample drawn from one group describes that group only.
Data shows **what** happened, not **why** — a rise in the numbers does not by itself show what caused the rise.
Data collected in the past does not say what will happen in the future.
A conclusion about something that was never measured is never supported, no matter how much data was collected.
steps: Name the group the data actually describes
Check the conclusion stays inside that group and inside what was measured
Quote the statistics that support the conclusion

foundation.question_text:
The table shows the mean and the range of the amounts, in dollars, raised each week by two Year $8$ fundraising teams over a term.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Team}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline \text{Blue}&96&48\\ \text{Gold}&112&20\end{array}$
The fundraising trophy goes to the better team. Which team should get it? Give two reasons.
foundation.solution_text:
$112 > 96$
Gold has the higher mean, so Gold raised more per week on average.
$20 < 48$
Gold has the smaller range, so Gold was also steadier from week to week.
**Gold should get the trophy**, because both statistics point the same way.

foundation.question_text:
The table shows the mean and the range of the numbers of library books borrowed per student last term by two Year $7$ classes.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Class}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline 7\text{A}&14&9\\ 7\text{B}&17&22\end{array}$
Ravi says that $7$B is the better borrowing class in every way. Is Ravi correct? Use both statistics in your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
$17 > 14$
$7$B has the higher mean, so $7$B borrowed more books per student on average.
$9 < 22$
$7$A has the smaller range, so $7$A's students were much more alike in how much they borrowed.
**Ravi is not correct**: the data supports $7$B being ahead on average, but $7$A is the more consistent class.

Half of $60$ is $30$, and $18 < 30$, so **A** is false.
Soup received $6$ votes, and the survey asked each student for one choice rather than what they like, so **C** is false.

foundation.question_text: The SRC asked the $24$ students in one Year $7$ class which day the sports carnival should be held. $15$ of them chose Friday, so the SRC concluded that most of the $900$ students in the school want Friday. Is this conclusion supported by the data? Explain.
foundation.solution_text:
The data describes only the $24$ students in that one class.
Those $24$ students are a sample of the $900$, and one Year $7$ class cannot speak for every year group in the school.
**Not supported** — the data supports a conclusion about that class only.

foundation.question_text: For one week a school counted the items placed in its recycling bins: paper $480$ items, bottles $310$ items and cans $155$ items. The principal concluded that students care more about recycling paper than about recycling cans. Is this conclusion supported by the data? Explain.
foundation.solution_text:
The count records how many items went into each bin, and nothing else.
How much students care was never measured, and a school uses far more paper than cans anyway, so more paper items is exactly what you would expect.
**Not supported** — the data measures items collected, not attitudes.

foundation.question_text: Every one of the $118$ students in Year $9$ was asked which event they would enter at the sports carnival. Athletics was chosen by $44$ students, more than any other event. Sana concludes that athletics is the most chosen carnival event among Year $9$ students at her school. Is her conclusion supported? Explain.
foundation.solution_text:
The population is the $118$ Year $9$ students, and every one of them answered, so this is a census of Year $9$.
A census covers the whole population, so the result is exact for that population rather than an estimate.
**Supported** — athletics really is the most chosen event in Year $9$.

foundation.question_text: $40$ of the $600$ students at a school were chosen at random and asked how many books they borrowed from the library last month. Their mean was $3.5$ books. Write a conclusion about the school that this data supports.
foundation.solution_text:
The $40$ students were chosen at random from all $600$, so every student had the same chance of being picked and the sample fairly represents the school.
The sample mean was $3.5$ books.
**A supported conclusion** is that students at the school borrowed about $3.5$ books each from the library last month.

The graph falls from $70$ to $60$ between Weeks $2$ and $3$, and from $100$ to $90$ between Weeks $4$ and $5$.
**Two supported conclusions** are that more bottles were recycled in Week $6$ than in any other week, and that the number recycled did not rise every week.

foundation.question_text: Posters about recycling were put up in a school. In the four weeks before the posters went up, a mean of $42$ drink bottles per day were placed in the recycling bins. In the four weeks after, the mean was $58$ per day. Mia concludes that the posters caused the increase. Is her conclusion supported by the data? Explain.
foundation.solution_text:
The data shows that the mean rose from $42$ to $58$ bottles per day, so it does support the conclusion that more bottles were recycled after the posters went up.
Nothing was recorded about **why** the number rose — warmer weather, a new bin position or a class competition would explain it just as well.
**Not supported** — the data shows what changed, not what caused the change.

development.question_text:
The table shows the mean and the range of the numbers of books borrowed each week from three sections of a school library over a term.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Section}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline \text{Fiction}&84&31\\ \text{Non-fiction}&62&12\\ \text{Graphic}&79&45\end{array}$
Write a conclusion about which section is borrowed from most, and a separate conclusion about which section's borrowing is steadiest. Quote the statistics you use.
development.solution_text:
$84 > 79 > 62$
Fiction has the greatest mean, so fiction is the section borrowed from most, at about $84$ books each week.
$12 < 31 < 45$
Non-fiction has the smallest range, so non-fiction borrowing is the steadiest from week to week.
The two conclusions describe different things, so both can be true at the same time.

development.question_text: To find out what the $760$ students at a school want in the canteen, the SRC chooses $80$ students at random from the school roll and asks them. $52$ of the $80$ choose a hot-food day. The SRC concludes that most students at the school want a hot-food day. Is this conclusion supported? Explain.
development.solution_text:
The $80$ students are a sample, not a census, so any result is an estimate rather than an exact figure.
They were chosen at random from the whole roll, so every year group had the same chance of being picked and the sample fairly represents the school.
$52$ out of $80$ is well over half.
**Supported as an estimate** — because the sample represents the school, it is reasonable to conclude that most of the $760$ students want a hot-food day.

development.question_text: Every student in class $8$C was asked how many hours they spent on their class science project. The mean was $4.2$ hours. The school newsletter reports that 'students at this school spend about $4.2$ hours on their projects'. Explain what is wrong with the newsletter's conclusion, and write a corrected version.
development.solution_text:
Only the students in $8$C were asked, so the data describes $8$C and no one else.
Every other class in the school was left out, and their projects may take a very different amount of time.
**The newsletter's conclusion overreaches**, because it stretches one class's result to the whole school.
A corrected version is 'students in $8$C spend about $4.2$ hours on their class science project'.

The graph records only the five months up to June that have already happened.
The totals rise and fall — up to $180$, down to $150$, up to $240$, then down to $210$ — so there is no steady pattern to continue.
**Not supported** — past data cannot tell you what a month that has not happened yet will bring.

development.question_text:
Two groups want to claim that most of the $640$ students at a school would use a new bike rack.
Group A asks all $640$ students, and $354$ say they would use it.
Group B asks $30$ students standing at the existing bike racks after school, and $28$ say they would use it.
Which group's data supports the claim, and why does the other group's data not support it?
development.solution_text:
Group A collected data from every student, so their collection is a census of the school.
$354$ out of $640$ is more than half, and a census gives the exact figure rather than an estimate.
Group B asked only students who were already at the bike racks, so their sample is made up of students who ride to school.
**Group A's data supports the claim**, while Group B's $28$ out of $30$ describes bike riders and not the whole school.

development.question_text:
The table shows the mean and the range of the amounts, in dollars, taken each hour by three stalls at a school fete, over the six hours the fete was open.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Stall}&\textbf{Mean}&\textbf{Range}\\ \hline \text{Cakes}&58&22\\ \text{Drinks}&71&46\\ \text{Books}&44&9\end{array}$
Write two conclusions this table supports, and explain why 'the drinks stall was the best stall' is not one of them.
development.solution_text:
$71 > 58 > 44$
The drinks stall has the greatest mean, so it took the most money per hour on average, about \$71.
$9 < 22 < 46$
The books stall has the smallest range, so its takings were the steadiest across the six hours.
'Best' has not been defined, and the two statistics point to different stalls, so the table on its own does not support calling any one stall the best.

development.question_text: Every student at a school was asked how many minutes they spent in the library last week, and the mean was $46$ minutes. The librarian concludes that the students who spent the longest in the library are the school's best readers. Is this conclusion supported? Explain.
development.solution_text:
Every student answered, so the data is a census and it describes the whole school exactly.
What it measured, though, was time spent in the library, and reading ability was never measured at all.
**Not supported** — a conclusion can only use what was actually measured, even when the data covers everybody.

mastery.question_text:
For one term the SRC weighed the paper recycled each week by two year groups.
$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Year}&\textbf{Mean (kg)}&\textbf{Range (kg)}\\ \hline 7&18.4&6.2\\ 10&21.5&15.8\end{array}$
The SRC writes: 'Year $10$ is the school's best recycling year group, and this proves that older students care more about the environment.' Judge each part of that statement, quoting the statistics.
mastery.solution_text:
$21.5 > 18.4$
Year $10$ has the higher mean, so Year $10$ did recycle more paper per week on average, and that much is supported.
$6.2 < 15.8$
Year $7$ has the far smaller range, so Year $7$ was much steadier from week to week, and calling Year $10$ simply 'best' ignores the statistic that favours Year $7$.
Only two year groups were weighed, so nothing at all follows about the other year groups in the school.
The scales measured kilograms of paper, not how much anyone cares, so the second part of the statement is about something that was never measured.
**The first part is only partly supported, and the second part is not supported at all**.

$2 \times 60 = 120$
$130 > 120$, so entries in $2025$ really were more than double the $60$ entries in $2021$ and conclusion **1** is supported.
The graph records how many students entered each year, never why they entered, and entries actually fell from $100$ to $90$ in $2023$, the very year the house-points system began.
Other explanations, such as a new event or a bigger year group, fit the graph just as well, so conclusion **2** is not supported.
$2026$ is not on the graph at all, and the totals rise and fall rather than following a steady pattern, so conclusion **3** is not supported either.

mastery.question_text: A school wants to know how many library books its $700$ students read last month. Ben asks the first $50$ students who walk out of the library, and their mean is $7.2$ books. Zoe asks $50$ students chosen at random from the school roll, and their mean is $2.4$ books. Ben concludes that students at the school read about $7.2$ books each last month. Explain why Zoe's data supports a conclusion about the school and Ben's does not, and state the conclusion Zoe's data supports.
mastery.solution_text:
Both students collected a sample of $50$ from a population of $700$, so both results are estimates rather than exact figures.
Ben's $50$ all came out of the library, so every one of them is a library user, and the students who never go to the library are exactly the ones left out.
Those missing students would read the fewest books, so Ben's mean of $7.2$ is pushed far too high to describe the school.
Zoe chose her $50$ at random from the whole roll, so students who use the library often, rarely or never all had the same chance of being included.
**Zoe's data supports the conclusion** that students at the school read about $2.4$ library books each last month, while Ben's supports a conclusion about library users only.
